newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumer prices rise 0.3 percent in October.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumer prices rise 0.3 percent in October.

text.p: Consumer prices rose moderately in October, the Labour Department said Thursday, as the slowing economy did little to generate troubling inflationary pressures.
The department said the Consumer Price Index rose 0.3 percent after being up an identical amount in September.
With the often volatile food and energy sector excluded, the so-called core rate was more subdued, rising 0.2 percent after being up 0.3 percent in the prior month.
The rise in both the overall and core rate were identical to Wall Street estimates.
"All the numbers were about in line with expectations," Astrid Adolfson, first vice president and senior economist at MCM Moneywatch Inc., said.
"The inflation data were up in areas where it was expected and down in autos, where it was expected. (The CPI was) so in line with consensus it couldn't be better."

The new data on inflation came just one day after the policy-setting Federal Reserve Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave interest rates unchanged in the face of generally quiet inflation despite what many believe is full employment.
"The CPI number is right on expectations. It suggests the inflation picture is fine," Marilyn Schaja, a money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp., said.
The Labour Department said that food and beverage prices rose 0.6 percent after being up 0.5 percent in September. The rise reflected increases in beef and veal as well as fresh vegetables.

Energy prices gained 0.7 percent after being unchanged in in September with gasoline also increasing by 0.7 percent. Fuel oil, however, jumped 7 percent, the largest rise since January, when it rose 8.8 percent.
New vehicle prices fell 0.2 percent in October after jumping 0.6 percent in the prior month, while apparel and its upkeep rose again by 0.5 percent, identical with September.
Airline fares, which rose 2.1 percent in September, increased another 1.9 percent, while all transportation costs were up only 0.1 percent after rising 0.5 percent.
Medical care costs rose 0.2 percent, the same as in September, continuing a pattern of relatively modest increases.
Housing was up 0.3 percent after being up 0.2 percent in September.

At the same time, the department gave new evidence of the strength of the employment picture, saying the number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell by 4,000 to 328,000 in the week ended Nov. 9.
The four-week moving average, a more accurate representation of employment trends, also fell, declining by 3,500 to 330,250.
